2005A16.goal: Subtract a two-digit number's digit sum from it; the result ends in $6$. Count such numbers. Write the number as $10a+b$.
2005A16.approach: The result is $9a$, which ends in $6$ only for $a=4$ ($36$). Then $b$ is free: $40$–$49$.

check.q: How many two-digit numbers have tens digit $4$?

2005A16.shortcut: A number minus its digit sum is always a multiple of $9$.
2005A16.recognize: Number minus digit sum: place value makes the units digit vanish.

2005A17.goal: The star's five segment sums use the numbers $3,5,6,7,9$, each at two segment ends. The sums form an arithmetic sequence; we want its middle term.

tools.name: Double counting
tools.why: Each letter is on exactly two of the listed segments.

tools.name: AP middle term
tools.why: A 5-term arithmetic sequence is symmetric about its middle.

2005A17.approach: The five sums total $60$, so the middle term is $12$.

steps.title: Total
steps.explain: Each letter appears in two of $AB,BC,CD,DE,EA$. Total $=2\cdot30=60$.

check.q: Five terms of an AP sum to $60$. What is the middle term?

solution: Sum of the five segment sums $=60$.
2005A17.shortcut: No need to find the actual arrangement.
2005A17.recognize: Sums over a cycle: each element counted the same number of times.

2005A18.goal: Best of five (first to $3$). Given B won game $2$ and A won the series, we want $P(\text{B won game 1})$. Use conditional probability.

tools.name: Conditional probability
tools.why: Compare the two cases for game $1$.

2005A18.approach: Case B won game $1$: A must win the next $3$: $\tfrac18$. Case A won game $1$: from $1$–$1$, A wins with $\tfrac12$. Ratio $\tfrac{1/8}{1/8+1/2}$.

steps.title: Cases
steps.explain: B 2–0: A needs $3$ straight: $\tfrac18$. Tied 1–1: A wins with $\tfrac12$.

check.q: If B leads $2$–$0$, what is $P(\text{A wins the series})$?

2005A18.bridge: Compare the two cases' probabilities of A winning.
solution: $P(\text{B won 1 and A wins})\propto\tfrac18$; $P(\text{A won 1 and A wins})\propto\tfrac12$.
2005A18.shortcut: Game $1$ was a fair coin, so both cases have the same prior weight; compare only the follow-up chances.
2005A18.recognize: "Given the outcome, what was likely earlier?": Bayes with simple case weights.

2005A19.goal: The middle of three unit squares is rotated $45^\circ$ and lowered until it touches the neighbours' top inner corners at $(\pm\tfrac12,1)$. We want the height of its top vertex $B$.
2005A19.approach: Bottom vertex at height $h$; its edges rise $\tfrac12$ over $\tfrac12$ horizontally, reaching the corners at height $1$: $h=\tfrac12$. Top vertex: $\tfrac12+\sqrt2$.

steps.title: Bottom vertex
steps.explain: The lower edges pass through $(\pm\tfrac12,1)$ with slope $\pm1$, so the bottom vertex is $\tfrac12$ lower: $h=\tfrac12$.

check.q: A line of slope $1$ through $(\tfrac12,1)$ meets $x=0$ at what height?
What is the diagonal of a unit square?

2005A19.bridge: Find the bottom vertex from the contact points, then add the diagonal.
solution: Contact points $(\pm\tfrac12,1)$ on edges of slope $\pm1$.
2005A19.shortcut: The rotated square's lower half is a right isosceles triangle; it sinks until its width at height $1$ is $1$.
traps: Assuming it rests on the line (bottom at $0$).
Using side length instead of the diagonal.
2005A19.recognize: Tilted squares resting on corners: use the $45^\circ$ slopes.

2005A20.goal: An equiangular octagon alternates sides $1$ and $\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$. We want its area. Extend the short sides to see a square with corners cut off.

tools.name: Corner triangles
tools.why: All angles are $135^\circ$, so the short sides are $45^\circ$ cuts.

tools.name: Subtraction
tools.why: The octagon is a square with corners removed.

2005A20.approach: Square side $1+\tfrac12+\tfrac12=2$, area $4$. Each corner triangle has area $\tfrac18$. Octagon: $4-\tfrac12=\tfrac72$.

steps.title: Bounding square
steps.explain: Each side of the square is a long side plus two legs: $2$.

check.q: What are the legs of a right isosceles triangle with hypotenuse $\tfrac{\sqrt2}2$?
What is the area of one corner triangle?

2005A20.shortcut: Equiangular octagons always fit in a rectangle with $45^\circ$ corners cut off.
traps: Treating it as a regular octagon.
2005A20.recognize: Equiangular octagons: box them in and subtract corner triangles.

2005A21.goal: For how many $n$ does $\tfrac{n(n+1)}2$ divide $6n$? Simplify the ratio.
2005A21.recognize: Divisibility of expressions: simplify the quotient to a fraction in one variable.

2005A22.goal: $S$: first $2005$ multiples of $4$ (up to $8020$). $T$: first $2005$ multiples of $6$ (up to $12030$). Common elements are multiples of $12$ that lie in both.

steps.title: Bounds
steps.explain: $S$ ends at $4\cdot2005=8020$; $T$ ends at $12030$. Common elements are multiples of $12$ at most $8020$.

check.q: What is the largest element of $S$?

2005A22.bridge: Multiples of $12$ up to the smaller maximum.
solution: Common elements: multiples of $12$ up to $8020$.
2005A22.shortcut: Every third multiple of $4$ is a multiple of $12$: $\lfloor2005/3\rfloor=668$.
2005A22.recognize: Intersections of arithmetic progressions: lcm, with the tighter upper bound.

2005A23.goal: Diameter $AB$, point $C$ with $BC=2AC$, $DC\perp AB$, and $DE$ a diameter. We want $\tfrac{[DCE]}{[ABD]}$. Both areas share the factor $DC$.
2005A23.approach: $[ABD]=\tfrac12\cdot2r\cdot DC=r\cdot DC$. $[DCE]=2\cdot\tfrac12\cdot OC\cdot DC=\tfrac r3DC$. Ratio $\tfrac13$.
2005A23.bridge: Both areas are multiples of $DC$; compare $OC$ with $r$.
2005A23.shortcut: No need to compute $DC$ — it cancels.
2005A23.recognize: Area ratios with a shared height: compare the bases.

2005A24.goal: $P(n)=\sqrt n$ means $n=p^2$ for a prime $p$. We need $n=p^2$ and $n+48=q^2$ with $p,q$ prime. So $q^2-p^2=48$.

tools.name: Same parity
tools.why: Their sum $2q$ is even, and the product is even.

2005A24.shortcut: $P(n)=\sqrt n$ forces $n$ to be the square of a prime.

2005A25.goal: $AB=25$, $AC=42$, $AD=19$, $AE=14$. We want $\tfrac{[ADE]}{[BCED]}$. Triangles sharing angle $A$ have areas proportional to the products of the sides around $A$.
2005A25.approach: $\tfrac{19\cdot14}{25\cdot42}=\tfrac{19}{75}$. The quadrilateral is the rest: $\tfrac{56}{75}$. Ratio $\tfrac{19}{56}$.
2005A25.bridge: Fraction of the big triangle, then compare to the remainder.
traps: Comparing to $[ABC]$ instead of the quadrilateral ($\tfrac{19}{75}$).
Computing areas with Heron's formula unnecessarily.
2005A25.recognize: Sub-triangles sharing a vertex angle: ratio of the products of adjacent sides.
